66186276B48953429733047.name: Idaho
66186276B48953429733047.summary:
Idaho carries the country's strictest criminalised restroom regime. Its 2026 facility-use law, effective 1 July 2026, makes it a crime for a trans person to use a restroom or changing room not matching their birth sex — in government buildings and in any private business open to the public, including gas stations, restaurants and hospitals — with a misdemeanour of up to one year and a felony of up to five years on a repeat within five years. Four successive legislative rounds ran from 2023 to 2026, alongside a ban on official recognition of Pride flags.

A federal lawsuit followed the law's passage; contemporaneous reporting states the law was partially blocked, leaving it in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists. Since then a March 2026 bill extending felony restroom penalties to all public accommodations has passed the House, a March 2026 forced-outting statute has been signed, a birth-marker freeze has been in effect since January 2026, and the federation's Supreme Court declined in 2024 to review the state's bar on gender-affirming care.

66186276B41335105066757.name: Louisiana
66186276B41335105066757.summary:
Louisiana posts the country's highest measured killing rate against trans women: 24.7 per 100k trans women per year reported, 11.6 recorded, on the TGEU trans-murder-monitoring base (428 US victims, 2008–2025) — a floor rather than a total, though the same analysis cautions that legal-risk rankings do not sort physical safety, and the top-ranked state records 23.5. In custody, a 45-year-old Black trans woman serving a life sentence was killed by other inmates at Angola prison on 2 April 2024, at least the 16th violent death of a trans or gender-expansive person that year; killings continued into 2026.

On 31 May 2026 a mob of about ten beat a trans couple, Aurora Rush and Shae Sanders, outside a women's restroom at a park in Benton; no attacker was arrested, while both victims were charged with disturbing the peace and Rush was jailed in a men's facility and searched by a male guard despite a female marker on her licence. On 15 July 2026 the Bossier Parish Police Jury unanimously approved — on the first of two required votes, reportedly at the sheriff's request — a local ordinance criminalising trans restroom use, described as one of the most punitive in the country. Louisiana has no statewide adult bathroom ban, so the parish ordinance is the state's sharpest instrument.

66186276B29106115751815.name: Texas
66186276B29106115751815.summary:
Texas operates one of the country's most actively enforced anti-trans regimes. Its facilities law (the SB 8 'Women's Privacy Act', in force 4 December 2025) produced enforcement within days: state troopers checked identification at women's restrooms in the Capitol while cities and campuses adopted sharply divergent compliance and evasion policies, and the attorney general opened the first state bathroom-law enforcement inquiry of its kind — against an Austin school district, escalated with a second records demand in April 2026 after a tip-line complaint.

Violence exposure is the national worst in absolute terms: 44 recorded killings of trans women over 2008–2025 (about 7.6 per 100k trans women per year; the monitoring project frames all rates as undercount floors). A July 2026 law-by-law legal-risk assessment grades Texas in its top 'Do Not Travel' tier.

Attorney General Paxton escalated his inquiry into Austin ISD (27 Apr 2026) with a second records demand over allegations a student used a bathroom inconsistent with their sex assigned at birth, after a March investigation opened via a state tip-line complaint alleging an SB 8 violation — the first state 'bathroom law' enforcement inquiry of its kind.

66186276B52324970173776.name: Tennessee
66186276B52324970173776.summary:
Tennessee is the only US state with a standing criminal ban on gender-expressive performance: the Adult Entertainment Act (2023) criminalises 'adult cabaret entertainment' — defined to include 'male or female impersonators' — anywhere children could see it, at up to 11 months 29 days and a $2,500 fine for a first offence and a 1–6 year felony on repeat. The ban is enforceable: the Sixth Circuit revived it on standing grounds and the Supreme Court declined review (February 2025), so its constitutionality has never been decided on the merits; no prosecutions are publicly reported, but a civil-rights suit over a district attorney's threat to charge a 2023 Pride event remains ongoing, and a visitor presenting in drag faces live charging exposure rather than a dead-letter law.

Since 2026 the state has also mandated birth-sex placement in prisons and shelters, and its ban on gender-affirming care for minors was constitutionally upheld by the Supreme Court in June 2025. Killings of trans women run at 7.8 per 100k per year — above the general national homicide rate.

Mulroy, leaving the appeals-court dismissal in place and the Adult Entertainment Act enforceable; notes a separate ACLU suit on behalf of Blount County Pride remains ongoing after a district attorney general threatened prosecutions over a 2023 Pride festival.

State-by-state Trans Murder Monitoring analysis (2008–2025): Tennessee's rate of killings of trans women is 7.8 per 100k/yr — above the general national homicide rate (~6.0) — with all state rates framed as undercount floors that do not sort by legislative-risk category.

66186276B64014601259366.name: Kansas
66186276B64014601259366.summary:
Kansas's SB 244 (signed February 2026) is among the harshest instruments a traveller can meet: it confines trans people to birth-sex facilities in government buildings, voids Kansas-issued IDs with corrected markers (licences invalid from 26 February 2026, no grace period, holders notified), and creates a private right of action under which anyone may sue a person they suspect of a violation for about $1,000 — a bounty-style exposure that the February 2026 legal-risk assessment singled out as the cycle's first 'Do Not Travel' addition, warning it 'could meaningfully affect interstate travel'.

Two trans men sued within days of enactment (Doe v. State of Kansas, with civil-liberties counsel), citing fear of violence under the law; a May 2026 injunction covers only the healthcare provisions, leaving the facility and ID regime in force.

66186276B65591139260314.name: Florida
66186276B65591139260314.summary:
Florida's 2023 law (Fla. Stat. 553.865) makes it a second-degree criminal trespass — up to 60 days — to remain in a public bathroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth after a government employee orders departure; the ACLU of Florida calls it 'complex, confusing, and vague' and of limited actual coverage, and among at least 14 states with facility restrictions only Florida and Utah criminalise the act itself.

Equality Florida and the Human Rights Campaign have issued named travel advisories warning of risks to trans travellers and movers.

Physical safety is comparatively better than the law suggests: a July 2026 analysis puts Florida's recorded killing rate for trans women at 3.7 per 100k per year, below the average of the worst-law states — itself an undercount floor.

72843720B863019116732.name: Centro
72843720B863019116732.summary:
The region contains two of the six regions with the highest recorded counts of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence in the 2012-2025 region-by-region study maintained by the country's principal LGBT monitoring project.

Against that stands the strongest judicial response to transphobic violence recorded anywhere in the country: in January 2025 a first-instance court in this region's main university city recognised a "transphobic motive" in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the association that supports trans sex workers, and - for the first time - admitted the national trans-movement organisation as civil party.

For a visitor the combination is specific: the highest-frequency regions of the country's violence record are here, but so is a documented court that named transphobic motive and ordered reparation.

sources.summary: Dire news-agency report (24 Jan 2025): a Bologna first-instance court recognised a "transphobic motive" in the punitive rape of a trans sex worker, sentenced the perpetrator, awarded damages to the victim and to the trans-movement association that helps sex workers, and for the first time admitted the Movimento Identita Trans (MIT) as civil party - the strongest judicial recognition of transphobic aggravation recorded in this country.

Progetto Gionata region-by-region study of anti-LGBT hate-motivated violence 2012-2025: names the Italian regions with the highest victim counts, six of them ranking at the top; Lazio and Toscana (both inside Centro) are two of the six highest-victim regions, alongside Lombardia, Piemonte (Nord-Ovest), Campania and Puglia (Sud). Provides the per-region violence distribution used to score all Italian units.

72843720B863019116732.modelContext: Rome/Florence/Bologna: the institutional heart — Rome's scene is large if more discreet than Milan, Bologna historically Italy's most LGBT-friendly city (Arcigay birthplace, leftist municipal tradition), Tuscany tourism envelope; central regions combine visibility with the strongest civil-society infrastructure.

82249235B4167839012994.name: New Brunswick
82249235B4167839012994.summary:
New Brunswick is the clearest Canadian case of a provincial government reversing course on trans rights within one election cycle. Policy 713 (2020) originally protected 2SLGBTQIA+ student privacy and inclusion. In July 2023, the Higgs government amended it to require parental consent for under-16 name/pronoun use, triggering protests outside the legislature. The Holt government reversed the amendment on 19 December 2024, effective 1 January 2025: parental consent is now "encouraged but no longer required" for the informal use of chosen names and pronouns by students of any age (it remains required for formal use in official records for students under 16), with a "presumed capacity" concept based on child-and-youth-advocate recommendations. The revised policy text extends its application to the whole school environment, including "visiting professionals, student teachers, parents, volunteers, and visitors", so current school rules technically reach non-residents present in classrooms.

Deviation: 0.02 below the national score of 0.86. The reversal is a strong positive institutional response — a government that legislated against trans students repealed the provision after one term. The residual signal is the demonstrated capacity for hostile policy within an election cycle and the 2023 protest period, which create a slightly higher baseline of political volatility than provinces that never legislated against trans people. No street-level disruption of public expression events was documented.

Compared to Alberta (0.76) and Saskatchewan (0.79), New Brunswick is materially higher: it did not use the notwithstanding clause, and its hostile policy was reversed rather than immunised from judicial review. Compared to the national score, the gap is small and time-sensitive — the current effective policy is protective, and further reversal would bring New Brunswick to or above the national level.

31927357B1137737933275.name: Puebla
31927357B1137737933275.summary:
Puebla led the national statistics for 2025 with 7 recorded killings of LGBT+ people; trans women constituted 58.3% of all such killings nationwide that year, across at least 17 states reporting victims. Its legal-gender-recognition law (2021) keeps an 18-year minimum-age requirement that the Supreme Court voided in March 2022, yet the state congress has still not corrected the text — legislative non-compliance with a final court ruling is itself a hostility signal directly relevant to a visitor whose documents must match presentation. There is no dedicated investigative machinery, no transfeminicide offence, and no state-level enforcement data.

The combination of top-of-table lethality and open defiance of the judiciary distinguishes Puebla from states that simply lack statutes: here a statute exists but the legislature actively refuses to conform it to a binding ruling. Context for comparison: Mexico City, which also had high counts in 2024-25, created a transfeminicide investigation unit and mandatory-response protocol within months; Estado de México, which likewise defies a Supreme Court ruling on recognition, has at least had a penal-code hate-crime provision covering bias motives since 2021. Puebla has neither the court-compliant text nor any criminal-law protection or enforcement innovation.

1811400B57209440839078.name: Tripura
1811400B57209440839078.summary:
This state shows the country's clearest pattern of border-checkpoint profiling of gender-nonconforming presentation. In August 2024 police reported apprehending 15 Bangladeshi nationals including seven transgender people in separate incidents within 24 hours, one group seized at a highway check post en route to India's financial capital, some described by police as "disguised as third-gender" - the explicit frame that trans presentation is a cover for infiltration. A coordinated November 2024 sweep detained twelve more, including minors and transgender people. The state shares a long, porous international border, which sustains the checkpoint geography. These are named-state-actor operations with published counts, directly facing any trans-presenting visitor crossing by land.

The institutional counterweight is nominal: the state is one of only twelve states/UTs to have constituted a transgender welfare board under national rules, but a right-to-information investigation found most such boards leaderless or inactive, with no compliance mechanism and no real power. On the audited record there is no statute criminalising trans presence here; the documented harm is police practice at the checkpoints.

Primary count for the August sweep.

Northeast Today report (2 Aug 2024): seven Bangladeshi nationals apprehended at the Panisagar check post on the Agartala highway en route to Mumbai — per the article, two transgender individuals plus others police described as "disguised as third-gender" persons. The source of the explicit disguise framing.

Sentinel Assam report (9 Nov 2024): in coordinated operations across Tripura over 24 hours, twelve Bangladeshi nationals including minors and transgender people were detained; a post-midnight group of six included three transgender persons, destined for Mumbai. Establishes the pattern recurring months after the August cluster.

Press Information Bureau, Government of India (8 Dec 2021, Ministry of Social Justice & Empowerment): state-wise list of the 12 states/UTs that had constituted Transgender Welfare Boards under section 10(1) of the Transgender Persons Rules 2020 — Tripura included. Official record of the board's existence.

The Quint RTI investigation (5 Nov 2024) into state Transgender Welfare Boards: most of the 12 constituted boards lack a compliance mechanism or real power and were found leaderless or inactive — the basis for treating board existence as nominal rather than an offset to border profiling.

1811400B32673734874058.summary:
West Bengal replicates the Tripura checkpoint script: South Dinajpur police arrested a Bangladeshi transgender person for allegedly "infiltrating India," treating trans presentation as evidence of illegal entry rather than identity; police also detained the e-rickshaw driver who carried her from the border. The state shares a long Bangladesh border and falls within the same policing logic. West Bengal is also one of only three states recording cases under the Transgender Persons Act in 2021 (3 of 7 nationally), indicating some legal infrastructure exists but also that trans-targeted crime is occurring at a detectable rate.

Against the national 0.43, West Bengal sits −0.09. The border profiling is visitor-facing and state-actor-driven, but the incidents are fewer and less concentrated than Tripura's repeated-sweep pattern. Compared to Tripura (0.31), West Bengal's harm is a single documented arrest plus the broader infiltration framing rather than repeated mass operations; compared to Delhi (0.38), which shares the profiling language but also has India's strongest institutional trans presence, West Bengal lacks that offsetting civic infrastructure outside Kolkata.

A welfare board exists (one of 12 states/UTs with a constituted body), but per the RTI investigation it operates without a functioning policy framework. For a foreign visitor transiting the land border, the primary exposure is the same appearance-as-suspicion-trigger mechanism documented in Tripura.

Compared to Kerala (0.50), Tamil Nadu adds the explicit court commendation and longer institutional history; compared to Punjab (0.35), which saw a religious authority veto trans public assembly, Tamil Nadu's state machinery actively protects it. A trans visitor at the Kumbh is inside an institutionally recognised religious hierarchy, not a marginalised underground. The inclusion is contested, however: a rival leadership instalment drew protests from within the community and other sects, gurus threatened to boycott the 2037 Kumbh, and a top-ranking trans monk who objected was physically attacked on 12 February 2025. UP also has a constituted welfare board.

Against the national 0.43, UP sits +0.03. The Kinnar Akhara inclusion is visitor-facing, seasonal, and institutionally validated by the broader Akharas' governance structures, but the festival-week attack and boycott threats show the recognition is contested rather than settled. A further counterweight exists — a single transgender woman, Kajal, was strangled in Kanpur (Aug 2025) during a robbery — but this is a lone incident with no patterned state-actor response and does not constitute a regional finding under the single-incident rule. Compared to Tamil Nadu (0.53), UP lacks a comprehensive policy framework or judicial endorsement; compared to Maharashtra (0.38), UP does not show the festival-entry religion-screening that creates outing mechanisms at public gatherings. The net positive is narrow and temporally concentrated.

1811400B70654311394581.name: Chhattīsgarh
1811400B70654311394581.summary:
Chhattisgarh mirrors Maharashtra's garba screening: in Bastar district, VHP and Bajrang Dal members objected to non-Hindu sponsors and participants at garba events, claiming damage to "cultural purity," and pressed religion-gated entry conditions — tilak applied to participants, Hanuman Chalisa recitation before start, and a Varaha-avatar poster circulated to organisers — with at least three garba nights called off and tickets cancelled after written objections; police received a memorandum and arranged venue security. It is the same outing mechanism as in Maharashtra, minus the Aadhaar document checks: a religion-screened gate at a public festival examines and outs gender-nonconforming visitors via actors who are not supposed to be involved. Unlike Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh has no constituted transgender welfare board (absent from the 12-state/UT list). Additionally, in November 2024 a transgender woman, Kajal (alias "Coca Cola"), was stabbed to death and dumped in an abandoned quarry in Baloda Bazar district in a Rs 12 lakh contract killing over rival claims to a community leadership seat ("guru gaddi") — a single incident with no sourced second instance, recorded for pattern awareness rather than as a decisive factor.

Against the national 0.43, Chhattisgarh sits −0.06. The combination of festival-entrance screening (visitor-facing, seasonal, outing mechanism) and the absence of any state welfare apparatus distinguishes it from Maharashtra (0.38), which carries the same screening but at least has a board. Compared to Tripura (0.31), whose harm is state-police-driven border detention, Chhattisgarh's exposure is community-organiser-driven at private-adjacent festivals and the violence is a single unresolved incident. The gap to the national score is modest and confidence moderate.

14911670B7632012573600.name: Ceara
14911670B7632012573600.summary:
Ceará is the most consistent lethal hotspot for trans and travesti people in Brazil's Northeast: 11 killings in 2024 — the region's highest toll and third nationally (G1, 28 January 2025, on the ANTRA dossier) — and 8 in 2025, tied with Minas Gerais for the highest state total of that year's 80 nationwide (Igbá Agência, 26 January 2026; SBT News). The 34% national drop is not read as improvement by ANTRA's leadership, since violence reappeared as attempted homicides (at least 75) (SBT News).

There is no state-level legal distinction: the federal constitution and penal code apply uniformly. What sets Ceará apart is sustained lethal exposure, and the national victim profile sharpens it for a visibly trans traveller — 97% of victims are travestis and trans women, over half aged 18–29, 70% of those with recorded race are Black, 97% killed in public spaces with most incidents outside capitals. Two consecutive years at the top of the ranking indicate an entrenched environment rather than a statistical blip.

Igbá Agência report (26 Jan 2026) on the 9th ANTRA dossier: Ceará recorded 8 killings of trans people in 2025, tied with Minas Gerais at the top of the state ranking; Brazil total 80 — 18th consecutive year as the country killing the most trans people; of the 57 cases with race recorded, 40 (70%) were Black; the Northeast took 38 of 80; killings fell ~34% from 122 in 2024, which the dossier attributes to violence migrating into attempted homicides rather than to improvement.

14911670B91095571793858.name: Rio Granda do Norte
14911670B91095571793858.summary:
Rio Grande do Norte recorded zero trans killings in 2024 but jumped to 4 in 2025—the sharpest deterioration in the ANTRA dataset. Against a population of ~3.5 million, four cases yields approximately 1.14 killings per million per year, the highest per-capita rate among all 27 units in 2025 and roughly three times the national figure of ~0.38/million. The dossier cautions against reading a single-year zero as safety and notes the volatility.

This rate-driven exposure puts RN about 0.11 below the national 0.71. Compared with Ceará (0.61), RN's absolute count is lower (4 vs 8) but the per-capita risk is actually higher; the deviation from national is therefore slightly larger than one might expect from the raw numbers. The state sits within the Northeast bloc that accounted for 38 of 80 national killings in 2025.

No state-level statutory restriction or unique legal finding applies; the risk is purely a violence-rate signal. For a visitor, the small absolute numbers mean a single incident dramatically shifts perception, and the volatility suggests the environment can turn rapidly.

19177384B97722443848736.name: Buenos Aires
19177384B97722443848736.summary:
Buenos Aires Province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in Argentina: the federal human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police—or by third parties under police cover—against trans and travesti people during operations in La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría, carried out under "preventive policing" frameworks. Academic legal analysis (CELS CEDAW shadow report; UNLP/Pensamiento Penal) confirms that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased use of drug-law prosecution (devolved to provincial justice in 2005) and street-offence law as the operative instrument for indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity—a patterned, state-implicated escalation with impunity.

The deviation from the national score (0.58) is −0.05. No other province has a comparable volume of multi-source, patterned enforcement documentation reaching the UN treaty-body system. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework (drug-law devolution + anti-narcotics security policy) that measurably increased police persecution of trans women. Protective institutions coexist—the provincial defensoría maintains a 2024 registry-rectification guide and documents discrimination caseloads—but these are resident-facing and do not offset the visitor-facing exposure to arbitrary detention during any police stop.

Compared with Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires (0.55), the Province lacks CABA's tribunal contravencional judicial-oversight structure and anti-discrimination apparatus; its police-judge model under the código de faltas gives less post-detention review. Compared with the silent majority of provinces (national score), the difference is one of documented pattern rather than statutory hostility—no BA law criminalises gender identity, but enforcement practice does the work.

17162690B44985096553766.name: Subcarpathian Voivodeship
17162690B44985096553766.summary:
Subcarpathian (Podkarpackie) is the epicentre and last holdout of Poland's "LGBT-ideology-free" resolution wave. It was one of five voivodeships adopting a regional anti-LGBT declaration (repealed 20 September 2021 only after the European Commission threatened to freeze its regional development funds), and its Łańcut county held Poland's final surviving anti-LGBT charter of the family until its extraordinary-session repeal on 24 April 2025—six years after the phenomenon began. The capital, Rzeszów, saw its mayor Tadeusz Ferenc outright ban the 2019 Equality March on security grounds; the district court later overturned the ban and the march proceeded, but the executive intent to exclude a visible LGBTQ public presence is on the record.

The resolutions were never criminal statutes, but the repeal was extrinsic (EU funding leverage) rather than a change in local attitudes, meaning the de facto social climate that produced them persists. For a visitor, the practical exposure is being visibly trans at a public event in an eastern Podkarpackie town where the local authority resisted all external pressure until 2025.

Score of 0.42 sits 0.10 below the national 0.52. Well below Łódź (0.48), which also carried a voivodeship-level resolution but produced neither a march ban nor a five-year institutional holdout. This is the deepest sub-national negative in Poland's dossier.

17162690B23777949290372.name: Podlaskie Voivodeship
17162690B23777949290372.summary:
Podlaskie saw Poland's most violent assault on a public LGBTQ event: at the 20 July 2019 Białystok Equality March, roughly 1,000 marchers were attacked by thousands of far-right and football-hooligan groups who attempted to block the route. Police detained 25 people; 32 counter-demonstrations had been registered that day, including a prayer vigil at the Cathedral Basilica. In the run-up, Archbishop Tadeusz Wojda had a proclamation read in every church across the region. The surrounding Białystok County had been declared an LGBT-free zone in 2019, though the city itself did not adopt one, and its mayor questioned whether the march was "needed" while the PiS city council filed a motion to stop it.

The state's protective response improved materially: at the fourth Equality March (28 September 2024), ~300 participants were escorted by 500 police officers and the Podlaskie police reported zero incidents. This is positive evidence under the single-incident rule (institutional learning, proportionate deployment), but it does not erase the 2019 pattern—organised mass violence met with a partial 25-person detention response, embedded in a documented church-and-county mobilisation infrastructure.

Score of 0.44 sits 0.08 below the national 0.52. Slightly above Subcarpathian (0.42), which lacked Podlaskie's demonstrable five-year improvement in state protection, but below Masovian (0.56), where the institutional machinery runs the other way.

Regional news report (28 September 2024): about 300 people took part in the fourth Bialystok Equality March under the slogan 'to live without fear', protected by 500 police officers; counter-demonstrations formed at several points on the route but the voivodeship police reported no incidents after the march - organisers stressed showing LGBT+ people as part of the local community.

17162690B69262761487853.name: Lublin Voivodeship
17162690B69262761487853.summary:
Lubelskie carried a voivodeship-level "LGBT-free" resolution from 2020 until its 20 September 2021 repeal under European Commission funding pressure. Its municipality of Świdnik (population ~40,000) was the first local authority in all of Poland to adopt an anti-LGBT resolution (March 2019, "against homopropaganda, LGBT ideology and the early sexualisation of Polish children"), and its deputy council chair explained the act explicitly as opposition to Warsaw's LGBT+ Declaration signed a month earlier. Świdnik became the template copied by roughly 100 authorities nationwide.

The resolution is now formally gone, but as with other eastern voivodeships the repeal was coerced rather than converted—the underlying civic mobilisation that produced Poland's first-ever anti-LGBT charter persists as a de facto signal. No march violence or ban is documented at the voivodeship scale beyond the general resolution-era hostility.

Score of 0.45 sits 0.07 below the national 0.52. Above Subcarpathian (0.42), which additionally produced a mayoral march ban and held out until 2025, and above Podlaskie (0.44), where the 2019 coordinated mass assault adds a violence dimension absent in Lublin. Below Małopolska (0.48), which pairs its resolution history with Kraków's clearly positive institutional trajectory.

17162690B67655395900928.name: Lesser Poland Voivodeship
17162690B67655395900928.summary:
Małopolska adopted a voivodeship-level "LGBT-ideology-free" resolution in 2020, repealed on 20 September 2021 under EU funding pressure, placing it in the same five-region configuration as the eastern belt. The regional declaration carried the same intent as its siblings: to exclude a visible public LGBTQ presence from the voivodeship's civic space.

Within the same unit, however, Kraków—the capital and Poland's second city—has moved decisively the other direction. In May 2024 newly elected mayor Aleksander Miszalski announced he would become the first Kraków mayor ever to attend the city's LGBT Equality March and would fly a rainbow flag at city hall. His predecessor Jacek Majchrowski (2002–2024) had only become an honorary patron of the march in 2021 and never attended. For a visitor in Kraków's old town, the operative institutional signal is the mayor's public presence, not the repealed voivodeship document.

Score of 0.48 sits 0.04 below the national 0.52: the resolution history pulls it down, Kraków's positive trajectory prevents a deeper drop. Above Lublin (0.45), where no equivalent capital-city counter-signal exists, and well above Subcarpathian (0.42), where the capital actively banned a march. 17162690B84565288021286.name: Masovian Voivodeship
17162690B84565288021286.summary:
Masovian, anchored by Warsaw, is the institutional counterweight to Poland's eastern resolution belt. On 6 February 2024, Warsaw's Voivodeship Administrative Court repealed the last remaining "against LGBT ideology" document in the country. Warsaw is the origin point of the progressive response: in February 2019 Mayor Rafał Trzaskowski signed a 12-point LGBT+ Declaration (security, education, culture, sport, employment; drawn up with LGBT NGOs, including an intervention hostel and school "lighthouse keeper" projects), which provoked the first anti-LGBT municipal resolution (Świdnik, March 2019) as an explicit counter-reaction. The administrative-court campaign, led from Warsaw by the national Commissioner for Human Rights and carried through the provincial administrative courts and the Supreme Administrative Court, dismantled the resolution network nationally.

The unit's dark stain is historical: in May 2005 the city under mayor Lech Kaczyński banned that year's Parada Równości, and the ECtHR in Bączkowski and Others v. Poland (2007) ruled the ban violated Articles 11, 13, and 14 ECHR. This is 20 years past and has not been repeated; the current institutional trajectory is clearly positive.

Score of 0.56 sits 0.04 above the national 0.52. The only unit scoring above national in this dossier; well above Małopolska (0.48) and the eastern belt (0.42–0.45), where the resolution legacy dominates and no equivalent court-repeal or declaration infrastructure exists.

27671186B7584771598694.name: Bauchi
27671186B7584771598694.summary:
Bauchi sits in the twelve-state Sharia criminal bloc of northern Nigeria, and it is where that system's ultimate penalty was actually pronounced: in June 2022 a Sharia court in Ningi sentenced three men — including a 70-year-old — to death by stoning for same-sex acts after arrest by the Hisbah religious police, reportedly the first time a death sentence has actually been imposed for homosexuality in Nigeria. The sentence was pronounced, not carried out; no execution is on record.

The appellate counterweight is real but fragile: the state's Upper Sharia Court quashed two stoning death sentences in 2003 (denial of counsel, defective confession), and Amnesty International recorded a string of similar successful appeals. A June 2025 country-of-origin note confirms the code remains in force, and corporal enforcement of Sharia morality law in Bauchi continues to be cited in 2025–26 advisory material.

Zamfara is where Nigeria's Sharia criminal-law wave began: its governor introduced the Sharia Establishment Law on 27 October 1999, in force 27 January 2000, and by 2002 eleven more northern states followed — a parallel system of Sharia courts with criminal jurisdiction over Muslims, which the 2025 government country-of-origin note confirms is still operative and capital-punishment-capable for same-sex acts. A 2019 rights-monitoring study of 173 Sharia-court cases from 2017 uses Zamfara as one of three sample states, confirming the courts function in practice, not just on paper.

No capital sentence is on record as imposed in Zamfara, and no trans-specific incident appears in the dossier; the finding is pioneering the bloc's enforcement architecture and hosting functioning religious courts.

Borno is one of the twelve northern Nigerian states applying Sharia criminal law in parallel with the federal system since the 1999–2002 wave. A June 2025 government country-of-origin note lists Borno among the states where the Sharia penal code remains in force for Muslims, criminalising same-sex acts between men (death penalty the maximum) and between women (penalties up to flogging and imprisonment), with a dedicated section on enforcement and the religious police — the legal architecture, not a case record, is the finding.

No trans-specific incident, no Hisbah case and no court-level study covers Borno in this dossier; the bloc's own reporting caveat is that enforcement data capture only a fraction of actual cases, so silence is not evidence of safety. The federal criminal code's coverage of men's acts (up to 14 years) applies here as everywhere in Nigeria.

27671186B8148656125930.name: Imo
27671186B8148656125930.summary:
Imo combines community violence with active state policing against gay people. In April 2018 a crowd in Isiala Mbano stripped two men accused of gay sex, beat them and paraded them through the streets with palm leaves tied around them; a follow-up report records that police took the two men in custody. In February 2025 the state police command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at a hotel in Owerri, arresting eight suspects and charging them under the 2014 anti-homosexuality law, citing its 14-year term — the command's briefing expressly framed the enforcement as covering a 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act'.

The pattern runs across years and across modalities: mob justice met without accountability in 2018, and named, state-command enforcement invoking the criminal law in 2025. For a discovered visitor here, risk comes from neighbours and police alike.

The outlet situates the attack in a rising pattern of mob justice enabled by the 2014 anti-gay law.

Nigerian Newspoint report (19 February 2025): the Imo State Police Command announced it had stormed a 'same-sex party' at the Graziella Hotel, Orogwe, Owerri West LGA on 15 February 2025 after a hotel tip-off, arresting eight named suspects (four women, four men) and charging them under the anti-gay law the command cited as carrying a 14-year term; the command's briefing expressly framed enforcement against 'gay, lesbian, bisexual and/or transgender act', with fleeers still being sought.

27671186B63712480376187.summary:
In May 2018 in Ekpoma, a community discovered two men having sex; one was lynched to death and the other escaped. The coverage framed the act as an 'abominable' one defying 'the traditional laws and heritage of the land', and no prosecution is recorded: customary moral judgement operating lethally, with complete impunity. For national context, a rights-monitoring report published in January 2025 documented 556 violations against real or perceived LGBT people affecting 850 victims across Nigeria in 2024 — and states these are only a fraction of the true scale.

Edo's finding is the Ekpoma killing itself: where a discovered visitor can face lethal 'community justice' invoked in the name of tradition, answered afterwards by nobody.

65028918B93184959873838.name: Aceh
65028918B93184959873838.summary:
Aceh is the only province in this country operating a codified religious criminal law of its own: the Qanun on jinayat (No. 6/2014) criminalises same-sex conduct (liwath, musahaqah) and close proximity (khalwat), with public caning as its signature punishment, applied by Islamic Shariah courts and policed by the Wilayatul Hisbah religious force alongside the secular Satpol PP units. Enforcement is active and widening: in August 2025 a Sharia court — sitting behind closed doors — sentenced two men to 80 strokes each for hugging and kissing, caned in a public park before around 100 spectators, with eight more people caned the same day; up to 100 strokes are available for morality offences generally, and Amnesty International called the practice 'state-sanctioned discrimination and cruelty'.

The Qanun does not name transgender people, but enforcement reaches them: a February 2025 boarding-house round-up detained a waria and a gay student facing up to 100 strokes under the liwath provision, with officials urging landlords to police tenants; in January 2018 police detained twelve transwomen and shaved their heads to teach them 'how to act like real men'. Private consensual conduct that carries no criminal penalty in any other province here can be publicly caned by a court in Aceh.

West Papua scores identically to Papua (0.11) and sits below the enacted-regulatory provinces West Sumatra (0.12) and South Sulawesi (0.12), where the risk is administrative or legislative rather than physical-state violence, and below Jakarta (0.12), where police overreach drew strong rights-group condemnation.

76434192B26311534340602.name: KwaZulu-Natal
76434192B26311534340602.summary:
KwaZulu-Natal is where documented street violence against queer people meets the country's most powerful traditional authority. A 2024 criminology study from a university in the province documents queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu, a township north of Durban — daily life in which the constitutional guarantee of equality does not reach. In January 2012 the Zulu King's anti-gay remarks at a harvest festival made the collision explicit: the royal house insisted the reported 'rotten' wording was a mistranslation; the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate; the provincial premier backed the royal family; and the Congress of Traditional Leaders of South Africa (CONTRALESA) responded that the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network demanding an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and was 'only seeking fame'.

For a discovered visitor, the province's pattern is that local moral authority — monarchy, chiefly councils, and the provincial government siding with them — has publicly ranged against queer claims, while academic documentation shows queerphobic violence persisting in its townships.

sources.summary: University of KwaZulu-Natal, Criminology and Forensic Studies MA thesis (Buthelezi, 2024): 'A criminological exploration of queerphobic violence and victimisation of self-identifying queer sexual minorities in KwaMashu Township' - documents violence against queer people in a Durban-area township despite the Constitution's equality guarantee, situating it within South Africa's pervasive crime and hate-crime context.

Pink News report (26 January 2012) on the fallout from Zulu King Goodwill Zwelithini's anti-gay remarks at a harvest ceremony: the royal family called the reported 'rotten' wording a mistranslation, the South African Human Rights Commission said it would investigate, the KwaZulu-Natal premier backed the royal family, and CONTRALESA said the Pietermaritzburg gay and lesbian network that demanded an apology had shown the king 'disrespect' and were 'only seeking fame'.

76434192B92524600968894.name: Mpumalanga

Mpumalanga is where the country's official house of traditional leaders launched its organised campaign against constitutional equality for queer people. Meeting at Hazyview in June 2010, the National House of Traditional Leaders and its provincial houses — while professing to 'respect' the Constitutional Court's same-sex marriage judgment — resolved that 'traditional leaders are disappointed that this immoral practice has been given a lifeline by our courts', declared their opposition to legal recognition, warned of ostracism and violence, and vowed a five-year campaign against it. Reporting in 2016 documented the same body asking Parliament to review the constitutional clause that protects people from discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation.

This is official traditional-structure hostility, taken on this province's soil and stated as durable climate rather than enacted law: there is no provincial statute against queer people, no enforcement against visitors, and no retrieved Mpumalanga-specific trans-incident series. The finding is the platform the country's chiefhood announced here — and did not retract.

76434192B37104984973577.name: Limpopo
76434192B37104984973577.summary:
Limpopo's rural life runs through chiefs and traditional courts to a degree that makes the parallel customary-law system the province's defining risk factor. Human Rights Watch's analysis of the legislation at issue warned that it 'establishes a separate legal system for people living in the former Bantustans' and 'threatens to undermine this security for millions of South Africans living in rural areas', 'particularly for the exercise of gender and sexual rights' — because chiefs and traditional courts adjudicate personal-status and morality-adjacent matters under customary law, with a consent presumption running against the individual. The later record, from a 2025 verification pass: the bill was enacted as the Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act of 2019, and was then declared unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court in 2023, with the declaration suspended and the Act's validity extended while Parliament works on a replacement. A 2012 activist report — 'culture of the chiefs threatens our rights' — pressed the same case contemporaneously.

No statute criminalises a visitor's expression here and no trans-specific incident series is recorded. But for an outed visitor in rural Limpopo, the practical moral authority is often the chief's court rather than the ordinary court — and that jurisdiction's record on gender and sexuality runs against the individual. The absence of recorded incidents reflects under-reporting, not demonstrated safety.

76434192B69392740373411.name: Gauteng
76434192B69392740373411.summary:
Gauteng — the province containing Johannesburg and Pretoria — is where the country's protections are most visibly operational. It hosts the first representative quantitative study of hate crimes against gay and lesbian people ever conducted anywhere in this country (2003/04, by an LGBT well-being institute with a university applied-psychology centre, documenting prevalence, consequences and contributing factors, with the era's leading community organisations as partners). A 2016 national campaign review confirms only three such studies exist in the country's history, placing Gauteng squarely in the small tier of provinces where the evidence, reporting channels and NGO capacity demonstrably exist. There is no province-specific ban or enforcement action here: the national constitution enumerates sexual orientation, and the equality statute and hate-crime framework operate uniformly, with the courts, prosecutors and civil society that apply them most concentrated in this province.

One caveat cuts both ways: the province's comparatively high recorded hate-crime volume — the very reason the evidence exists — may partly reflect better reporting infrastructure rather than greater danger. The operational conclusion stands either way: an incident a visitor reports here is likeliest to meet a functioning institutional response.

19338628B22645672383103.name: Île-de-France
19338628B22645672383103.summary:
Île-de-France sits fractionally below the national 0.67, but the deviation is small because the negative and positive factors largely cancel for a traveller. On the negative side, the Paris agglomeration and urban units over 200,000 inhabitants concentrate 55% of anti-LGBT offences for 43% of the population—a rate of 9 per 100,000, more than double the rural 4 (2025 update: 54% for 43%, still 9 per 100,000 against the rural 4 and national 7). The 2025 Marche des Fiertés was mobilised under a heavy police frame; the self-declared "gay patriot" collective Eros sought to march with prefectural backing, Inter-LGBT threatened to cancel if it participated, and participants reported that "the Marche des fiertés is becoming a sensitive event." A visitor attending the Pride encounters organisational tension and a security apparatus that signals vulnerability even as it protects.

On the positive side, the 9-per-100k rate is heavily inflated by reporting propensity, community visibility, dedicated police liaison desks and the density of associations—all of which mean more incidents are recorded and responded to, not necessarily that a visitor is at greater risk; Paris alone records 22 per 100,000 but the official note cautions that offences there also involve non-residents (commuters and tourists). Île-de-France has the country's densest trans support infrastructure and the largest community, giving a discovered visitor the best odds of institutional help and social buffer anywhere in metropolitan France.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The dossier's own caveat is explicit: "high recorded rates in Paris should not be read as Paris being dangerous." Compare with Bourgogne-Franche-Comté (0.62), where the state actively banned assembly; Île-de-France's state response to Pride was protective if tense. Compare with PACA (0.65), which shares the metro-rate exposure but adds the Fréjus dress-code incident as a specific negative on public appearance.

19338628B95725112529620.name: Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur
19338628B95725112529620.summary:
PACA deviates −0.02 from the national 0.67. The region-specific negative is the RN mayor of Fréjus, David Rachline, issuing an arrêté on 1 August 2023 prohibiting swimming on communal beaches for anyone wearing "covering and loose clothing"—a dress-code order whose language directly reaches gender-nonconforming public appearance. However, the Toulon administrative tribunal suspended the arrêté and condemned the commune to €3,000 in August 2023, a clear institutional pushback. Per the enforcement-over-statute rule, a court-blocked municipal order carries small weight; its residual harm is the chilling signal it sends to a visitor who sees public dress policed by mayoral fiat, even if the specific order no longer operates.

PACA also shares Marseille's metro exposure: urban units over 200,000 record 9 per 100,000 anti-LGBT offences against the national average of 7, a pattern driven by reporting density and visibility as much as by elevated actual incidence. The region's net position mirrors Île-de-France (0.65): a small negative from a specific municipal incident partially offset by a strong judicial correction, set against an urban-rate backdrop that the dossier explicitly cautions against reading as danger.

Compare with Hauts-de-France (0.64), where the RN pattern spans multiple communes and "around thirty associations" without a comparable single court suspension to offset it; PACA's one documented arrêté was fully and quickly reversed. Compare with Bourgogne-Franche-Comté (0.62), where the prefecture's ban was upheld rather than overturned—a materially different judicial outcome that justifies the spread between 0.62 and 0.65.

28173009B98838729156012.name: Chechnya
28173009B98838729156012.summary:
Chechnya's security apparatus operates outside legal constraint on this question. In February 2017, law-enforcement and security officials launched an anti-gay purge: dozens of men were rounded up and held in unofficial detention facilities, starved and tortured; some were forcibly disappeared; others were returned to their families 'barely alive from beatings' after their captors exposed them to relatives encouraged to carry out honour killings (Human Rights Watch, 2017). Independent domestic reporting in January 2019 found the persecution resuming and the documented secret facility active again, while the regional leader's press office denied such sites exist. Since 2022, two investigations have documented detained homosexual men blackmailed into 'volunteering' for front-line conscription in Russia's war in Ukraine (at least seven sent, one killed) and a mass wave of unlawful detentions tied to forced mobilisation. The UK Home Office note (June 2025) records systematic campaigns in this republic and the wider North Caucasus from 2017 to 2024 — abductions, torture, extrajudicial killings — and assesses trans people and visible advocates as likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, with such violence spreading beyond the region after the 2023 'extremist movement' designation.

For a discovered or outed visitor: detention without legal process, torture, coerced conscription or death, with no functioning judicial remedy.

28173009B24428243574749.name: Dagestan
28173009B24428243574749.summary:
The UK Home Office country policy note (June 2025) identifies the North Caucasus — including Dagestan — as a zone where LGBT+ people are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, documenting systematic campaigns by Chechen and North-Caucasus authorities between 2017 and 2024 including abductions, torture and extrajudicial killings. North Caucasus SOS's director states there is “no safe life for LGBTIQ+ people in the North Caucasus”, that even private existence can trigger violence, detention or forced return to families, and that the situation worsens year on year.

Canada's travel advisory tells travellers to avoid all travel to Russia, names Dagestan among the republics where terrorist attacks are frequent, and warns that special permission from the Ministry of the Interior is required to enter certain areas — an access regime that also hampers independent monitoring of how state and customary authority operate on the ground.

For a visitor the risk here is the regional pattern: the federal ‘extremist’ designation of 2023, which extended violence in detention beyond the region, combined with local security structures and family-honour norms that produce extrajudicial responses unmediated by legal process. No separate Dagestan-specific written law targeting trans people exists, and no Chechnya-scale documented purge infrastructure is attributed to this republic.

28173009B19676032168465.name: Moscow
28173009B19676032168465.summary:
Moscow is where the federal anti-LGBT framework is enforced most visibly. The Moscow Times' 2025 survey of persecution — headlined around “arrests, club raids and extremism charges” — records that the first person charged with creating an extremist organisation on LGBT grounds, Kotov, was arrested in Moscow in late December 2024; the paper reported Russia's first prison sentence under the LGBT-‘extremism’ designation in February 2025, an organising case following a ruling reported from Siberia in January 2025.

The severity of the federal law is uniform across the country, but enforcement intensity is not: Moscow concentrates the highest police density, the most active venue-level operations, and the bureaucratic touchpoints most likely to involve a foreign visitor — document verification, medical gatekeeping, registration procedures. For a trans visitor the practical result is a materially higher probability of encountering active enforcement of the same rules, and the country offers no protective institutional counterweight at any level.

28173009B76603557910928.name: Orenburg Oblast
28173009B76603557910928.summary:
Orenburg Oblast is the jurisdiction where the federal "LGBT extremism" designation first produced a criminal conviction against a commercial leisure venue. The Pose bar case (submitted to court July 2025 by the regional Investigative Committee) resulted in June 2026 in a seven-year sentence for owner Vyacheslav Khasanov, prison terms for two employees, and forfeiture of over one million rubles—the first criminal LGBT-extremism sentencing against a commercial venue in Russia (the first prison sentence under the extremism designation overall was handed down by a Siberian court in an organising case, reported January 2025, predating this one). The precedent establishes that a bar or club can be prosecuted as an extremist organisation, which is the scenario a foreign visitor walking into a commercial venue is most likely to encounter.

This is visitor-facing enforcement: the venue context (drinking, socialising) is exactly where a visiting trans person might interact with the criminal justice system. The deviation from national (0.12) is approximately 0.03 below. Comparable to Moscow (0.09), which concentrates raids and the first organiser prosecution; both represent active enforcement venues within the uniform federal law. Orenburg's specific finding—a seven-year sentence against a bar owner—sets the most severe commercial-venue precedent in the country.

36201628B69282955287113.name: NCR
36201628B69282955287113.summary:
The Philippines has no national anti-discrimination statute covering gender identity; the national picture is violence against trans women, documented in a 2024–2025 series of killings, without dependable local machinery. The capital region carries the country's strongest local protections: in July 2025 Quezon City became its first local government unit to enact a Gender-Inclusive Health Ordinance, creating a framework for gender-affirming primary care, mental-health support and specialist services through the city's public-health system — the only enforceable institutional recourse a discovered visitor can find anywhere in the archipelago.

Lethal violence is on the regional record too: the transrespectful memorial lists Shaina Bayabay, 29, strangled during a drinking session in Pasig City, Metro Manila, on 1 March 2024. Protection here is real but partial — a functioning framework on paper in the country's largest city, and an enforcement-and-services reality that does not yet extend past city limits.

For a transgender visitor the exposure is two-fold: the venues where trans women are concentrated in commercial sex work carry the highest violence and trafficking risk, and enforcement sweeps can sweep up anyone in the vicinity. 36201628B91065962446027.name: Western Visayas
36201628B91065962446027.summary:
On 10 October 2022 the Capiz State University Office of Student Affairs told students perceived as trans women that they would be barred from university premises unless they cut their hair and wore the uniform prescribed for males, delivering the instruction through campus guards with one week to comply and threatening that they could not re-enroll otherwise; the office attributed the order to the university president. A legal-NGO case study documents the students' subsequent advocacy campaign — backed by paralegals of national LGBTQ organisations, who pointed to an existing municipal anti-discrimination ordinance in Roxas City, Capiz, which the office dismissed as inapplicable — and its later milestone: the first openly trans woman graduating as university valedictorian with highest honours. This is a documented episode of institutional gender-expression policing in a provincial (not metropolitan) setting, reversed by advocacy.

No killings from the 2024-2025 national series occurred in this region. The campus directive is a resident-facing action rather than a mechanism a visitor encounters; its force as a region signal is that in a conservative provincial setting expression can be policed by institutional authority without an operational local recourse — unlike Central Visayas, this region has no protective ordinance cluster of comparable reach.

36201628B64564033926366.name: Ilocos Region
36201628B64564033926366.summary:
The Pangasinan provincial board certified and affirmed Municipal Ordinance No. 15, s-2023 of Bayambang protecting the rights of LGBTQI persons (Provincial Board Resolution No. 799-2024, session of 19 August 2024)—a provincial-level endorsement of a municipal LGBTQ+ protection ordinance in a conservative province. This gives a visitor in the Pangasinan corridor a local complaint route absent in most other regions.

Against that, the Abra and Ilocos Sur provinces within Ilocos Region host the Bodong Indigenous Allied Group (BIAG), a codified customary-justice system with its own dispute-resolution authority over "crimes and tribal-related offences," recognised by Philippine courts. No trans-specific bodong ruling or customary exclusion was documented, but the legal-pluralism structure means that in a rural Abra or Ilocos Sur dispute, the applicable institution may not be a Philippine court.

Net effect: +0.03 above the national score, modest because the protective ordinance is municipal and the plural-justice uncertainty is localized to specific provinces within the region. Compare Central Visayas (0.63), where the ordinance cluster is broader (city IRRs with UNDP backing, unanimous municipal votes) and there is no countervailing alternative-justice structure.

36201628B49646111072560.name: ARMM
36201628B49646111072560.summary:
In the Bangsamoro autonomous region justice is legally plural: the region's 2019 administrative code provides that it be dispensed in consonance with the Constitution, Shari'ah, and traditional or tribal laws (the clause is carried in the research dossier; the cached code excerpt does not reach it), while the national Code of Muslim Personal Laws of 1977 remains in force. In July 2026 the Bangsamoro parliament tabled a bill for a comprehensive Shari'ah justice system code extending to ta'zir criminal offences — the category under which morality offences are prosecuted in comparable systems. No source establishes that Philippine Shari'ah courts currently prosecute same-sex conduct or gender expression, and no such law has yet passed.

The Shari'ah court system is expanding nationally: three new judicial districts and twelve circuit courts beyond BARMM were created by law signed in August 2024, extending into majority-Christian areas, with further access legislation in September 2025 and a Supreme Court resolution in January 2026 to operationalise the Shari'ah High Court.

The finding for a trans visitor is structural rather than enforcement-based: a dispute could fall outside the civil courts altogether, in a jurisdiction actively legislating criminal religious law with no protective ordinance or civil-rights infrastructure documented in the region. Forward-looking, and bounded by the fact that the ta'zir code is a proposal, not a power in force.

68945753B94077674833362.name: Daegu
68945753B94077674833362.summary:
Daegu has hosted the country's second-oldest queer culture festival every year since June 2009 — organisers mark seventeen consecutive years 'without fail', run 'as a form of resistance against hate and discriminatory politics', the 2025 edition under the slogan 'We Will Not Be E(r)ased' on central Daegu's Dongseong-ro. Organisers cite a Supreme Court ruling on local anti-discrimination ordinances as confirming sexual minorities as citizens protected by the Constitution.

The festival draws a recurring, organised counter-mobilisation: in September 2025 a Daegu–Gyeongbuk conservative-Protestant umbrella convened its 17th annual 'National Assembly Against Queer', gathering roughly 3,500 believers from some 1,600 churches from Banwoldang station along a 450-metre stretch toward Gyesan intersection under anti-homosexuality slogans, timed against the festival. For a visible trans visitor the result is a concentrated confrontational environment during festival week; the event itself continues to take place annually despite interference.

68945753B85435209225479.name: Daejeon

In October 2021 the Daejeon District Court ordered cancellation of the Army's forced discharge of transgender soldier Byun Hee-soo, holding the military should have considered her a woman when reviewing fitness for duty — a ruling widely described as a landmark in the case brought to repeal the discharge decision.

On 24 June 2024, after the Ministry of National Defense reversed the Army's original 'natural death' classification and recognised the 2021 death as service-related, Byun was interred at the National Cemetery in Daejeon. Around 60 activists gathered to protest the burial, arguing her service did not qualify her for interment there: state recognition of a trans person at the national memorial ground, met with a small but public rejection in open space.

68945753B59172752195743.name: North Chungcheong
68945753B59172752195743.summary:
North Chungcheong (capital: Cheongju) is scored −0.02 below the national 0.71 on the basis of the Byun Hee-soo case and its institutional aftermath, with the single-incident caveat applied explicitly. Byun, 23, was found dead in her Cheongju home on 3 March 2021 (apparent suicide) following forced military discharge and during ongoing mental-health counselling at a centre near her residence. Initial police and Army handling classified the death as 'natural'; this was overturned only three years later (April 2024) when the Ministry of National Defense's Central Military Casualty Review Board recognised it as service-related. The wrongful initial classification is the evidence: it reflects an institutional denial of the connection between anti-trans policy and a trans person's death, corrected only after sustained advocacy.

Per the single-incident rule, one death cannot establish a Cheongju pattern, and no repeat violence data exists for this unit. It is included at −0.02 rather than zero because Chungcheongbuk-do is small enough for one nationally prominent case to carry weight, and because the institutional response (wrongful classification sustained for three years before correction) is a state-implicated finding. 82085004B70364588595557.name: Northern Territory
82085004B70364588595557.summary:
The Anti-Discrimination Amendment Act 2025 (No. 27 of 2025, assented 30 October 2025; Part 3 in force 27 July 2026) removed the civil provision making it unlawful to "offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate" a person in public on the basis of a protected attribute, including gender identity. The NT is the only Australian jurisdiction that has actively reversed anti-discrimination protection rather than extended it; the government framed the rollback as "restoring freedom of speech and religion." For a visitor, public verbal abuse or humiliation directed at gender expression is now deliberately outside NT law while other states have brought it inside.

Federal protections continue to apply uniformly: the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 covers gender identity in every state and territory, and NT hate-crime penalty enhancements for SO/GI-motivated offences (2022 amendment, effective 2023) remain in force. No criminal expression ban, no facility-access ban, and no conversion-practice-specific enforcement issue arises for a short-term visitor beyond the general federal framework.

Remote-area context amplifies practical risk: Alice Springs records approximately 2,600+ offences against a population of ~25,000, and trans community infrastructure in the NT is thin. A single domestic killing of a Tiwi Sistergirl (Darwin, October 2024) is recorded for completeness but is one non-patterned incident and does not support a regional violence finding on its own.

Vs the national score of 0.86, the NT sits 0.09 below: the deliberate legislative removal of the "offend, insult, humiliate" protection is the strongest negative sub-national signal in Australia, even though it is a civil-law rollback rather than a criminal prohibition. Vs Victoria (0.88), where the 2025 Anti-Vilification Act created the country's first criminal offence for public incitement against a trans person, the NT moved in the opposite direction in the same year.

82085004B60194602145168.name: Victoria
82085004B60194602145168.summary:
Victoria's Justice Legislation Amendment (Anti-Vilification and Social Cohesion) Act 2025, passed in April 2025, created both civil and criminal vilification offences and extended protection beyond race and religion to disability, gender identity, sex, sex characteristics and sexual orientation, plus personal association; the civil grounds commenced 15 April 2026. The state human-rights commission's explainer records public incitement against a trans person becoming criminally chargeable alongside civil recourse.

A coronial inquest into the deaths of five young transgender women in Melbourne during the pandemic — lead case Bridget Flack, missing December 2020 — found Victoria Police failed the search, and Coroner Ingrid Giles made nine recommendations including urgent investment in trans health care and reform of missing-persons risk practice; the government is reviewing them. The inquest documents a serious institutional failure; the 2025 legislation and the review process are the corrective response.

82085004B21656044714531.name: New South Wales
82085004B21656044714531.summary:
The Conversion Practices Ban Act 2024 (No. 19 of 2024, bipartisan, in force 4 April 2025) makes practices directed at changing or suppressing sexual orientation or gender identity criminal offences punishable by up to five years' imprisonment, including taking a person interstate or overseas for the purpose or engaging a provider outside NSW. A civil complaints scheme runs through Anti-Discrimination NSW. NSW also operates an explicit self-identification prison-placement policy, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

Against these strong legal protections, NSW carries a concentrated violence pattern. Kimberley McRae was killed in her Coogee apartment (January 2020); the accused admitted killing her after learning she was transgender and the case went to murder trial (NSW Supreme Court), a positive institutional response. Mhelody Bruno, a 25-year-old Filipina trans woman who had arrived in Australia approximately six weeks earlier, was strangled; her killer received only 22 months on a consensual-strangulation account that ABC reporting showed the court never heard contested. Two killings of trans women in the same state within roughly a year, with one adequate and one clearly inadequate sentencing outcome, is recorded as a pattern plus a contested institutional response, not as isolated incidents. NSW is a common-law state with no statutory bill of rights and no state-level anti-vilification offence comparable to Victoria's 2025 criminal provision.

Vs the national score of 0.86, NSW sits 0.02 below: the criminal conversion-practice ban and self-ID custody are strong positives but narrow in direct traveler-facing exposure (a typical tourist is unlikely to encounter a conversion-practice provider), while the violence-and-sentencing pattern is more relevant to a visitor's physical safety and shows both institutional capability (McRae murder trial) and institutional failure (Bruno 22-month sentence). Vs Victoria (0.88), which has the criminal vilification offence that NSW lacks, the two states trade different kinds of protection.

82085004B93533858076668.name: Western Australia
82085004B93533858076668.summary:
WA's Equal Opportunity Act 1984 protects the attribute of "gender history," defined as a person who "identifies as a member of the opposite sex by living, or seeking to live, as a member of the opposite sex." This is a narrower, medically-inflected, binary formulation than the "gender identity" language used in Victoria, Queensland and the federal Sex Discrimination Act. A non-binary or gender-nonconforming visitor may not meet the state-law definition and would rely solely on federal coverage for a state-level complaint. WA has no state anti-vilification offence (civil or criminal) and no statutory charter of rights binding public authorities.

Reform is underway: the Births, Deaths and Marriages Registration Amendment (Sex or Gender Changes) Act 2024 received assent on 26 September 2024, removing medical and surgical prerequisites for registration of a sex or gender change, with substantive commencement by proclamation. This feeds back into the scope of "gender history" for complaints purposes but is not yet fully in force as of the scoring date.

Vs the national score of 0.86, WA sits 0.02 below: the narrower protective vocabulary and absence of both a vilification offence and a rights charter mean the state-level safety net is thinner than in eastern states, even though the federal floor is unchanged. Vs Queensland (national, no deviation record), which has a Human Rights Act 2019 binding public authorities and a conversion-practice prohibition in force since 2020, WA lacks both structural review and the specific coercion safeguard.

82085004B40257551482390.name: Australian Capital Territory
82085004B40257551482390.summary:
The ACT Human Rights Act 2004 requires public authorities to act compatibly with human rights and enables courts to issue declarations of inconsistency, providing a legal review mechanism for a visitor who encounters discriminatory conduct by a police officer, public servant or state facility that is absent in common-law states without a charter (NSW, WA, SA, TAS). The ACT is one of four Australian jurisdictions with an explicit self-identification basis for prison placement, reducing the risk of inappropriate custody for a detained gender-nonconforming visitor.

No region-specific incident series, enforcement pattern or institutional-failure finding was identified in the dossier for the ACT. The absence of negative evidence, combined with the structural rights protection and self-ID custody rule, places the territory modestly above the national average.

Vs the national score of 0.86, the ACT sits 0.02 above: the rights statute and self-identification custody are genuine structural positives for a visitor who might interact with police or detention, and no countervailing regional finding offsets them. Vs Victoria (0.88), the ACT lacks Victoria's 2025 criminal vilification offence but also lacks Victoria's coronial finding of police failure toward trans women; the two jurisdictions reach the same small positive deviation from different evidence.

sources.summary: ABC Background Briefing survey (3 July 2020) of trans prisoner placement across Australian jurisdictions: NSW, Victoria, the Australian Capital Territory and Tasmania have explicit self-identification placement policies (with documented exceptions where authorities doubt 'authenticity' or cite security), Queensland/NT/SA are case-by-case, and WA has no dedicated policy; includes the Mara Ellis case of a trans woman held at a WA men's prison in prolonged segregation later sexually assaulted in mainstream placement; estimates up to 400 trans and gender-diverse prisoners nationally and notes elevated assault risk.

Human Rights Law Centre report 'Ending Strip Searching in Australian prisons' (2026, with trans-community group Flat Out and FIGJAM; only front matter and partial text retrieved): documents strip-searching practice and its disproportionate harms for trans, gender-diverse and Indigenous prisoners across Australian jurisdictions, underpinning how a detained gender-nonconforming visitor faces custody screening.

25490228B8471183517505.name: Castilla y León
25490228B8471183517505.summary:
Castilla y León is the only Spanish autonomous community that has not enacted any regional LGTBI or gender-identity law, a vacuum maintained across multiple legislatures. The PSOE-proposed ley de igualdad real y efectiva de las personas LGTBI+ (registered December 2024) only reached processing on 11 June 2025 after the governing PP abstained and Vox voted alone against; Vox is on record rejecting LGTBI subsidies in the region. The pending law is explicitly framed around stopping the sexilio—the documented exodus of LGBT people, especially young ones, from the region's rural areas to larger cities.

For a transgender visitor the practical effect of the legislative vacuum is the absence of a dedicated regional equality office, no institutional hate-crime observatory, and no region-specific administrative protocol for responding to gender-motivated incidents. National criminal law still applies and no criminal ban or facility restriction exists in Castilla y León, so the severity floor is set by the state. The deviation from the national score (0.88) of approximately −0.07 reflects the sub-national administrative coldness and rural exposure identified in the dossier as Spain's real fault line, not any region-specific criminal threat.

Compared to Madrid (0.84), which at least operated a trans law and an LGTBIfobia law before narrowing them, Castilla y León has never had the framework to narrow; the gap is legislative vacuum versus legislative rollback. Compared to Ceuta and Melilla (0.85), Castilla y León's deviation is larger because its rural geography compounds the absence of any protective infrastructure and because the sexilio pattern is regionally documented, whereas the Ceuta/Melilla finding is statute-book only with no incident evidence.

sources.summary: Europa Press (11 June 2025): the PP's abstention let the Cortes de Castilla y Leon open debate on the PSOE's 76-article 'ley de igualdad real y efectiva de las personas LGTBI+' - the region remains Spain's only autonomous community with no LGTBI regulation of its own; only Vox and the two non-aligned members voted against; the socialist sponsor stressed education-sector training, a sanctions regime for non-compliant administrations, and special attention to the rural 'double discrimination' faced by LGTBI+ people.

SalamancaHoy (20 December 2024): the PSOE group registered the proposicion de ley expressly framed on stopping the 'sexilio' - the documented exodus of LGTBI+ people, especially young ones, from the region's rural areas to larger cities - and on breaking 'a wall' in regional society; spokesman Tudanca told the governing PP 'there are no more excuses' since the state law already demands regional development.

Diario de Castilla y Leon (11 June 2025): take-up-for-processing vote analysed by parties - PSOE, UPL-Soria Ya, Podemos, Por Avila and ex-Popular Igea backed it, recalling the region is 'la unica comunidad sin una legislacion propia' (a 2021-drafted law remains blocked), with the socialist delegate noting rising assaults and hate speech since the far right entered institutions (former vice-president Garcia-Gallardo's rainbow-flag 'trapo' jab); the PP held rights are already guaranteed by the Constitution and Statute; Vox voted against alone; the LGTBI Participation Council chair warned the law must not be left 'empantanada' in process.

15666254B53975248776023.name: Kelantan
15666254B53975248776023.summary:
In August 2026 the Kelantan assembly passed a new Syariah Criminal Offences Bill — including a clause making gender change an offence for persons under the state's syariah jurisdiction — replacing provisions of the state's 2019 syariah criminal code that Malaysia's Federal Court had struck down as outside state power. The Bill also carries "protection of modesty" decency offences, backed by whipping (3–6 strokes), fines up to RM5,000 and imprisonment up to three years.

The sequence — invalidation by the federal courts, prompt deliberate re-enactment by the state assembly — documents institutional determination to criminalise gender transition, not a stray provision. The gender-change offence binds Muslims, including Muslim travellers exposed to syariah proceedings; the official climate it signals reaches all trans visitors.

sources.summary: The Star (12 Aug 2026): previews the new Kelantan Syariah Bill replacing the 16 provisions of the 2019 Enactment the Federal Court struck down — including 'protection of modesty' clauses making it an offence for a Muslim to fail to safeguard their private parts (whipping of 3-6 strokes plus fine up to RM5,000 or up to three years) alongside the clause criminalising gender change.

The Star (13 Aug 2026): reports the Kelantan assembly passing the strict new decency rules of the Syariah Bill — the enactment replacing the Federal Court–voided 2019 provisions, including the offence of gender change.

15666254B71460903090065.name: Terengganu
15666254B71460903090065.summary:
In May 2025 the Kuala Terengganu authority erected anti-homosexuality warning signboards at several locations, including near youth-frequented areas around a state university; when criticised, a state executive councillor publicly confirmed the installations were deliberate, framing them as a "constant reminder" to steer people away from homosexuality. A prominent transgender activist and, on 14 May 2025, thirteen civil-society organisations led by a national trans-rights group demanded removal, calling the boards discriminatory hate speech.

The state also retains hudud-style penal provisions (2002) that remain inoperative because a federal statute caps the sentences state religious courts may impose — confirmed current in a 2026 review — while discretionary syariah offences and the federal criminal prohibition of same-sex conduct do apply. What visitors meet here is open, ongoing official hostility, without any trans-status-specific criminalisation documented in the surviving sources.
