65028918B28366581005022.name: West Java
65028918B28366581005022.summary: The most concentrated wave of mob violence against transgender women in Indonesia: ten attacks on 45 victim-survivors in Bogor between 30 March and 15 July 2026, documented by Pelangi Nusantara — groups of 10–20 men punched, kicked, threw stones, glass bottles and firecrackers at trans women and stripped some of them naked, filming the assaults for social media under the account @bogorbersihlgbt ('Bogor clean of LGBT'). No alleged perpetrator has been publicly identified, arrested or prosecuted; a trans-rights activist who accompanied women filing police reports said officers 'accepted the case but worked on it half-heartedly,' and some survivors were too afraid to report. Separately, on 22 June 2025 police detained 75 people at a villa raid in the Puncak area of Bogor Regency at a gathering labelled a 'gay party' that violated no law — Amnesty demanded their release. Activists attribute the violence's legitimisation to Perpres 111/2025, which from October 2025 lists 'LGBTQ culture' as a national-resilience threat alongside terrorism and drug abuse: 'people feel able to commit violence arbitrarily because they believe the state has legitimised that violence.' The pattern-plus-impunity combination is West Java-specific; national same-sex criminalisation does not by itself explain the street-vigilante wave with total state inaction and explicit anti-trans branding over four months.

65028918B4119458748300.name: West Sumatra
65028918B4119458748300.summary:
The clearest enacted modern local anti-LGBT bylaw outside Aceh: Bukittinggi City Regional Regulation (Perda) No. 2 of 2024 on public order, articles 43-44, prescribes oral and written warnings, cessation of activities, social rehabilitation programmes, and administrative fines of Rp1,000,000 targeting LGBT people. 65028918B6690755070061.name: Bali
65028918B6690755070061.summary:
Bali is Indonesia's most tolerant mainstream environment: 2026 travel guidance still describes a "live and let live" ethos, with gay-friendly life concentrated in Seminyak, Canggu and Ubud, and no criminal enforcement against foreign tourists recorded. That informality, however, is not protection. The national penal code brought into force in 2026 criminalises extramarital sex, including same-sex relations; LGBTQ+ travel advisories rate the island "Exercise Significant Caution", public displays of affection are discouraged for all couples, and same-sex marriage remains unrecognised.

A 2025 ethnographic study of the island's trans women (transpuan) communities pointedly challenges the "refuge" framing, documenting persistent misrecognition and systemic discrimination beneath the tolerant surface. Visitors should read Bali as relatively safer by local custom — with the new penal code, conservative local administration and documented structural discrimination setting the limits of that safety.

65028918B16658067687714.name: Papua
65028918B16658067687714.summary:
No trans-specific legal measure or incident series is documented for this province in the surviving sources. The security environment, however, is not neutral: rights monitors recorded 138 acts of torture or ill-treatment in detention by police and military in the highland conflict zones of the island's western half between September 2021 and early 2025, "with almost no consequences", and a further surge of military deployments, fatal shootings and arbitrary detentions from August 2025, alongside internal displacement.

For any visitor — including a transgender one — contact with security forces in the highland districts carries a documented risk of arbitrary detention and mistreatment, and the surveillance environment raises the chance of being noticed and questioned. This is a general-population security finding, not evidence of trans-specific targeting.

65028918B9551391119865.name: South Sumatra
65028918B9551391119865.summary:
On 19 July 2026 Palembang's city government announced it was preparing a regulation rejecting LGBT, presented as local follow-through on Presidential Regulation (Perpres) No. 111 of 2025 on the national defence policy 2025-2029, which lists the 'spread of LGBTQ culture' among non-military threats; Mayor Ratu Dewa made the announcement in the courtyard of the Grand Mosque. The regulation remains in preparation, not enacted, with no specified penalty; no enforcement event is documented for this province. South Sumatra is one of the eight provinces analysed in OutRight's discriminatory-regulation mapping, and its neighbour Lampung saw a documented Satpol PP raid on three transwomen (November 2018) - the Sumatran belt is where local enforcement is consolidating.

The deviation from the national score is small and below it, similar to South Sulawesi (0.13). The Perpres 111/2025 framing elevates local anti-LGBT measures from moral panic to national-defence doctrine - the August 2026 ABC reporting links the 'rule that deems them a threat' to a wave of street attacks on trans women, though it cautions the trend cannot yet be confirmed - but without an enacted local penalty the traveler-facing risk here remains prospective. It sits above West Sumatra (0.11), which has a live bylaw with specified sanctions.

14339913B95766344400054.name: England
14339913B95766344400054.summary: Worse than the pre-2025 position, and worse than Wales on official posture. The EHRC's updated Code of Practice for Services, Public Functions and Associations was laid 21 May 2026 and came into force on 5 August 2026 as statutory guidance (replacing the 2011 code): single-sex spaces open to the public — toilets, gym changing rooms, hospital wards, rape-crisis centres — should be organised by biological sex, with trans people directed to gender-neutral or birth-sex facilities. The guidance binds service providers UK-wide but is administered in England, and it is the map's clearest 'you may be refused' signal. Its legal predicate is For Women Scotland v The Scottish Ministers (UK Supreme Court, 16 April 2025): 'sex' and 'woman' in the Equality Act 2010 mean biological/registered sex, and a Gender Recognition Certificate does not change legal sex for Equality Act purposes. The ruling has immediate visitor-facing consequences in England's transport and custody settings: following it, British Transport Police moved (17 April 2025, stated interim position) to strip-searching trans women detained on the rail network by male officers, reversing the acquired-gender policy for GRC holders. Anti-trans offending is statistically invisible in the official record: England and Wales reported 115,990 hate crimes in the year to March 2025 across five monitored strands, and transgender identity is not a separately recorded strand (unlike Scotland and Northern Ireland). The strongest practical gradient inside the unit is London — visible community, dedicated services, dedicated hate-crime policing — versus the rest of England; no sourced sub-England region-level evidence was found, so the unit is assessed whole.

sources.summary: BBC News (19 June 2026): a judge (Lady Ross, Court of Session) ruled Scottish Prison Service guidance allowing some trans prisoners to be housed by gender identity unlawful — sex segregation in prisons must be based on biological sex, applying the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 'definition of a woman' ruling. The judgment confirms the biological-sex custody logic that the same UK-wide ruling imposes on England's prison and custody decisions; the first minister said the government will consider the judgment (the Supreme Court had already held Article 8 confers no automatic right to opposite-biological-sex accommodation).

BBC News (5 February 2026): argument of the same judicial review, in which government lawyers said a blanket rule housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while For Women Scotland called the identity-based policy 'Orwellian'; the case tests how far the UK Supreme Court's April 2025 ruling (cited as the predicate for England's EHRC code and BTP strip-search policy) reaches into prison accommodation UK-wide.

82085004B13995298844162.name: Queensland
82085004B13995298844162.summary: Queensland is a protective outlier on the legal side: first in Australia to criminally prohibit conversion practices — Public Health Act 2005 ch 5B (s.213F), in force 20 August 2020, covering practices aimed at changing or suppressing sexual orientation or gender identity, with named prohibited techniques — and it drafted a complete anti-discrimination rewrite (Anti-Discrimination Bill 2024) with a modernised 'gender identity' attribute aligned to the Yogyakarta Principles, separated from sex-characteristics provisions, plus vilification offences; the rewrite was still in consultation in the documents reviewed. The one operationally adverse fact for a detained visitor is custody placement: Queensland sits outside the four self-identification jurisdictions (NSW, Victoria, ACT, Tasmania), so prison placement turns on surgical-intervention status or case-by-case assessment — meaning 'some trans women can be placed in men's prisons' here, unlike in the self-ID states.

sources.summary: Investigative feature (12 January 2018) on the plight of transgender women in French prisons: incarcerated on the basis of legal gender status, most trans women housed in all-male facilities because placement follows the sex on the ID document (Article D248 of the criminal procedure code separates men and women only); first-person accounts (a trans woman held in a northern correctional facility in 2014 shouted at by other detainees; another foreign trans woman detained after a publicised 2016 Paris protest trial); the controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty says transgender detainees - the majority of whom are women - are the group that 'suffers the most' in prison.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty (unofficial English translation) on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations of fundamental rights persist across all detention settings, based on some forty referrals since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, observations from the interior, justice and health ministries, and on-site/document inspections; recommendations extend to intersex and non-binary persons; follows an initial 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018), 'The Plight Of Trans Women In Prison': transgender women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender fall into a legal grey area and are punished for far more than their alleged crimes - first-person accounts of placement in an all-male facility (a three-day stay in Lille's men's prison in 2014, with detainee and staff hostility; an Argentinian trans woman's story of incarceration); Article D248 of the criminal procedure code assigns detainees by the sex on their ID; the controller-general of places of deprivation of liberty says transgender detainees are the group that 'suffers the most' in prison; also covers the well-publicised case of a US trans woman detained in poor conditions after a 2016 Paris protest case.

Opinion of 25 May 2021 of the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), unofficial English translation: official inspectorate opinion on the treatment of transgender persons in ALL places of deprivation of liberty; built on about forty referrals received since 2010, interviews with trans associations and European experts, and five on-site inspections (Fleury-Mérogis men's and women's prisons, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré, Toulouse-Seysses and the Toulouse central police station - eight trans women and one trans man interviewed); finds persistent serious violations of fundamental rights of trans detainees, isolation and overcrowding risks; recommends that the 2016 depathologising law (no more surgery requirement for civil-status change) be translated into prison regulations; explicitly extends to intersex and non-binary people.

36201628B45254163682963.name: Mimaropa
36201628B45254163682963.summary:
Mimaropa carries no region-specific laws against transgender people: no provincial ordinance criminalising expression or facility use is documented, and the framework that applies here is the national one — same-sex relations are legal, legal gender recognition does not exist, national equality bills have been filed repeatedly for decades without passing, while some cities and provinces have enacted local non-discrimination ordinances. Public homophobic and transphobic slurs are criminalised by the Safe Spaces Act, and school anti-bullying and gender-responsive education policies cover sexual orientation and gender identity.

Public acceptance is partial: a 2018 national survey found roughly one in five behind same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets, and executive orders creating a national diversity-and-inclusion programme remained unimplemented as of 2025 according to audited reporting. In mid-2025 a cluster of killings of trans people across several other provinces — a student found in a northern river, an activist shot in a southern city, another woman killed in the capital region — drew national calls to pass the stalled equality bill, documenting a pattern of lethal violence against a backdrop of unenacted protection. For a visitor, Mimaropa's profile is the national one: no state penalty for being trans, courts and local ordinances as practical recourse, and physical safety conditioned on setting and discretion.

68945753B85747362819570.name: Gangwon
68945753B85747362819570.summary:
No province-specific law, ordinance or enforcement pattern targeting trans people is documented for Gangwon; the framework a visitor meets there is the national one: being trans is not criminalised, and the courts are steadily tightening what legal gender recognition may demand — a May 2024 ruling ended any surgical requirement for changing registered sex, and in July 2024 a court held that police telling a trans person to avoid public restrooms for a while infringed their rights, awarding damages after both instances found for the claimant and an appellate court calling comfortable restroom use a fundamental and universal human right.

The same sources describe both the promise and the limit of that judicial route: a 2021 damages award against an academy that barred a trans student from restrooms shows recourse exists, while a 2021 national survey of 591 trans respondents — 41% using wrong-gender facilities out of fear, 39% restricting food and drink to avoid restrooms, 36% skipping facilities altogether — shows everyday facility avoidance remains the norm. For a visitor, Gangwon's audited record offers legality, functioning courts and no local hostility machinery, with social friction around public restrooms documented nationally rather than locally.

sources.summary: Korea Times (22 July 2024): the Seoul Central District Court ruled that a police officer's advice to an LGBTQ+ individual midway through legal gender change to "avoid using public restrooms for a while" infringed their personal rights; 300,000 won of a 3 million won claim awarded, final 2 July. Both first and second instances ruled for the plaintiff; the appellate court called comfortable restroom use "a fundamental and universal human right", and the officer received National Human Rights Commission human-rights education. Also cites the Commission's 2021 survey of 591 trans respondents (41% had used a restroom of a different gender than their identity out of fear; 39% avoided food and drinks; 36% forwent restroom use) and a 2021 Pohang branch ruling awarding 7 million won against an academy operator who barred a trans student from using restrooms.

1875124B91024374055933.summary:
The Public Ministry's 2012–2021 study places La Libertad second in absolute LGTB-homicide count (10 of 88 — after Lima's 12, level with Lima Norte), centred on Trujillo. The region's population share (~3%) is far smaller than its death share (~11.4%), giving a per-capita lethality roughly 3.8× the national average — a materially concerning concentration not explained by population alone, and placing the unit below the national score (0.36).

Counterweight: Ordenanza Regional N.° 009-2024-GRLL-CR (regional session 3 September 2024, approved 6 September 2024, published in El Peruano November 2024) promotes labour inclusion of travesti, transsexual and transgender people — their right to formal, dignified work in equitable conditions without discrimination on gender identity or expression, and recognition of the trans community as a vulnerable group. This is a resident-facing instrument (a visitor does not use it), but it evidences that this particular regional council legislated visibly for trans inclusion — the one such ordinance found in Peru's 26 departments. It also sits in the same department where rondas campesinas exercise recognised dispute-resolution authority, a structural caveat with no documented trans-specific case.

Net deviation: −0.02 from national. The per-capita violence concentration is the dominant factor; the ordinance prevents a larger deduction. vs Lima (now 0.38, above national): La Libertad's per-capita lethality remains worse, though Lima's higher absolute count and 2025 reporting case have lifted its score since the original comparison. vs Tacna (0.34): both are modestly below national, but La Libertad's multi-year dataset is more robust evidence than a single incident.

1875124B58976419670313.name: Tacna
1875124B58976419670313.summary:
On 19 April 2025 Marcia Paucara Cora, a 48-year-old trans woman, was found dead in a room of a hostel in central Tacna; the autopsy recorded death by mechanical asphyxia through compression of the upper airways. She had entered with a man who registered under a false identity and left alone roughly two hours later; police hold camera footage and taxi-driver testimony but, per the audited reporting, had not identified the suspect, and the case was being investigated as a possible hate crime. On 23 May her family and local LGBT collectives held a vigil describing the killing as the reflection of a structural system of violence.

The framework that reaches a visitor in Tacna in full: the audited reporting records that this country has neither a gender-identity law nor a hate-crime statute — so anti-trans violence can only be prosecuted as ordinary homicide, and the 'hate crime' label marks investigative posture, not a charge — and that a recently promulgated national law restricts public-bathroom access by reference to sexual orientation. Beyond this one incident and its response, no local ordinance, policing pattern against trans people, or municipal protection is documented; the investigating-as-hate-crime posture within a statute-less system is the audited local reality.

13589884B77991835419453.name: Atlántico
13589884B77991835419453.summary:
Caribe Afirmativo's 2025 annual report issues a specific, named warning of "increasing violence against LGBTIQ+ people in the Atlántico department," and quantifies it: 54 cases of intrafamily violence, 41 sexual offences, 12 discrimination cases, 8 digital-violence cases, 69 threats and 8 lethal-violence cases in the department, with 2 killings of LGBTIQ+ human-rights defenders; the report designates Barranquilla and Soledad as territories at "high" threat level. Barranquilla is the Caribbean-coast hub for trans sex work and the city where the NGO's documentation base operates, giving it both elevated exposure and visibility in monitoring data; the department appears explicitly in the 270-victim national total (+63% on 2024; one killing every 32 hours). Impunity is near-total nationally: 99.8% of threat cases never advanced past the investigation stage. A positive institutional signal is recorded: the department's development plan (and Barranquilla's) commits coordinated action with the prosecutor's office, police and judiciary to strengthen reporting, investigation and prosecution of violent acts against LGBTIQ+ people.

13589884B85526028135750.name: Risaralda
13589884B85526028135750.summary:
Risaralda carries no local statute aimed at trans people and no department-level incident entry in the audited record; what a trans visitor stands under is Colombia's national pattern. That pattern is violent and largely unpunished: armed groups circulated "social cleansing" flyers naming trans women as targets in 2024, at least 41 trans women were killed nationally in 2023 and 13 more in the first quarter of 2025, and of 155 criminal investigations into LGBTQ killings only 3 reached a verdict last year — roughly 2% against a 9% overall homicide-conviction rate.

State response to this violence is episodic rather than structural: the audited record shows a presidential order to investigate after a viral April 2025 murder of a trans woman in another department, vigils, and nothing resembling standing local protection machinery. Outside the largest cities the national figures are the operative risk for a visitor here.

1875124B3772980127380.name: Puno
1875124B3772980127380.summary:
Puno has no regional statute or incident of its own in the audited record, and the decisive facts are national — which means they apply in Puno like anywhere in Peru. In February 2025, Congress's Women and Family Commission unanimously approved bills (6506 and 8457) barring trans people from using public restrooms corresponding to their gender identity, with narrow carve-outs for medical care, custody and accompanying minors or disabled persons; in April 2025 the plenary approved the fused measure, waiving a second vote. A national human-rights institute published a detailed critique calling the measure institutionalised discrimination.

For a trans visitor the mechanism is therefore legal, not customary: restroom access is the flashpoint the law itself creates — its trigger was a complaint about toilet signage at Lima's airport — with no local variation documented for Puno.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): Congress's Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a bill barring trans people from public restrooms of the sex other than their birth sex (bills 6506 and 8457, by two governing-bloc legislators), with exceptions for custody situations, medical care, and accompanying elderly, under-12 or disabled people; the initiative also requires removing restroom signage ambiguous about who may enter. Trigger was a July 2023 complaint about gendered toilet labels at Lima's international airport. National law - applies in Puno as everywhere; still requires full plenary approval.

IDEHPUCP human-rights institute analysis (15 April 2025), 'Legalised discrimination': on 2 April 2025 Congress's plenary approved, waiving a second vote, the children's-sexual-rights law, fused by the Women and Family Commission with the trans bathroom-restriction bills; critiques the measure as institutionalised discrimination against trans people under national human-rights standards.

1875124B51528250409360.summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): the Congress's Women and Family Commission approved unanimously the dictamen of bills 6506/2023-CR (Montoya) and 8457/2023-CR (Muñante), which prohibit entry to public sanitary services designated to the opposite sex at birth (exceptions: custody, medical attention, accompanying a person under 12, an elderly person or a person with a disability) and prohibit ambiguous bathroom signage; the dictamen still required plenary support. Context: in July 2023 a complaint about the gendered signage at Jorge Chávez International Airport led to the labels being changed to 'mujeres/hombres en su diversidad'. Activist Gianna Camacho states no official statistics of trans violence in women's bathrooms exist, and enforcement would rest on individual security staff judging IDs.

IDEHPUCP bulletin, analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte (15 Apr 2025): on Wednesday 2 April 2025 the Plenary of Congress approved, exempting it from a second vote, the dictamen of the law strengthening the right to the sexual indemnity of children and adolescents (merger of bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR). Article 5.1 of the bill bans entry and use of public sanitary services to any person whose biological sex does not match the service's designated sex, with narrow exceptions for accompaniment/assistance and legal or judicial mandates. The bulletin reads the provision as a direct violation of equality and non-discrimination (Political Constitution art. 2.2, American Convention art. 1.1) in line with IACtHR OC-24/17, and as validating stereotypes about trans people.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024) on the Annual Report of the Observatorio de Derechos TLGBI of the Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia: 54 LGBTI homicides and 170 rights-violation cases between 2020 and 2023; more than half the homicide victims were trans women (30), then gay men (23) and one lesbian woman; yearly homicides 2020: 12 (8 trans women), 2021: 10, 2022: 13, 2023: 19 (12 trans women). Killings involved extreme cruelty (multiple gunshots, stabblings, throat-cuttings); rights violations peaked at 61 in 2020 (43 in 2022, 34 in 2023, 32 in 2021), trans women again the most affected. Includes testimony that in Feb 2023 extortion gang 'Los Gallegos' abducted sex worker Rubí Torres Silvano (31) in central Lima and killed her in Carabayllo with ~30 shots, a case of the pimping-mafia violence the movement identifies as the main trans-femicide driver.

An LGBTI activist quoted calls the measure discriminatory.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 October 2025): the leaked 11th Judicial Package would amend the penal code to criminalise conduct deemed 'contrary to biological sex and general morality' (up to 3 years' imprisonment), raise the minimum age for gender-affirming care from 18 to 25 with mandatory permanent infertility, punish providers with up to 7 years and patients with up to 3, and cover symbolic same-sex ceremonies (up to 4 years); 15 LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association opposed it. National policy, applies in this province as everywhere else.

Kaos GL Association (24 February 2026): LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025, 'The Year of the Family - A Major Siege', monitoring since 2007: 6 right-to-life violations (3 hate-motivated killings; trans people most affected), 89 torture/ill-treatment violations (51 in 2024), 313 liberty violations including 299 detention decisions, 67 private-life violations (16 in 2024, a substantial share obstructing trans hormone therapy), 540 expression/assembly violations (216 in 2024) including rainbow- and trans-flag bans. National data; no province-level breakdown.

19177384B49506124846693.name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
19177384B49506124846693.summary: Direction: mixed — the most legally protective jurisdiction in Latin America, with a repeating pattern of police round-ups of travestis and trans women in one neighbourhood. The city has operated its own anti-discrimination law since 1996, hosts a large visible scene and an LGBTQ-driven tourism economy, and concentrates the administration of the national employment-quota law for travesti, trans and transgender people alongside the national femicide/travesticide registry — it is where state response is most likely to be present. Against that: on 18 September, six months after an unlawful detention, officers from police station 18 carried out fresh detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications of travestis and trans women in the Constitución neighbourhood, writing several up under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code for lacking documents and arresting one — activists describe it as 'a new illegal procedure against travestis and trans', the third-plus iteration of the same operation in the same barrio, making it a pattern rather than a single incident. Nationally the climate has turned: 2025 set a record of at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity (+62% on 2024, one every 38 hours, the highest since monitoring began ten years ago), 32% of them inside police stations and penal facilities, with security-force violence multiplying from 17 cases (2024) to 64 (2025), trans women and travestis the majority of victims (142, 62.5%); federal closures of the equality ministry and the national anti-discrimination institute and dismissals of trans public-sector quota hires further erode recourse.

sources.summary: Washington Blade (10 April 2025): Argentine trans and travesti activists at a CABA rights forum (4 April 2025) describe their community's situation under the current administration as 'chaotic, desperate', with growing fear and vulnerability to violence, discrimination and poverty; the administration eliminated the Women, Gender and Diversity Ministry in December 2023, closed the national anti-discrimination institute (INADI) in 2024, and dismissed trans people the government had hired under the Trans Labor Quota Law (1% of public-sector posts). Named association honours Diana Sacayán, a trans activist stabbed to death in her Buenos Aires apartment in 2015, and Lohana Berkins, who died in 2016.

Agencia Presentes (19 March 2026), National Hate Crime Observatory data: 2025 was a record year — at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity, +62% on the previous year, one every 38 hours (highest since monitoring began ten years ago); perpetrators were mostly security-force members and unknown individuals in public spaces, with beating the most used modality; security-force violence cases multiplied from 17 (2024) to 64 (2025); 32% of 2025's crimes occurred in police stations and penal facilities (including a violent raid on a prison diversity pavilion that injured over 45 LGBT+ people and eight guards detained for beating a trans inmate); trans women and travestis were 62.5% of victims (142 cases); 64.8% of cases (147) were physical assaults (+101%), the remainder lethal — 16 murders (10 trans women), 53 structural-violence deaths and 11 suicides; in January 2025 a known stalker burned the home of lesbian activists, and a 55-year-old teacher was murdered in the Caballito neighbourhood in circumstances bearing hate-crime features the media did not frame as such.

14911670B90188072957077.name: Santa Catarina
14911670B90188072957077.summary: Direction: worse than national — the only Brazilian state to have enacted a statutory bathroom restriction, and the venue of a nationally decisive refusal. Lei 19.686 of 21 January 2026 requires every educational institution in the state — basic, fundamental, secondary, technical and higher — to provide bathrooms separately by sex, banning shared or unisex installation and use, with fines of up to R$10,000; a second bill approved 22 December 2025 extends the ban to state and municipal public administration bodies; a third, tabled October 2025, would restrict school and locker-room use to the sex recorded on the birth certificate — continued legislative escalation rather than a one-off. The nationally decisive case arose here: a trans woman was refused entry to the women's bathroom by staff at a Florianópolis shopping centre, urinated on herself in front of shoppers and had to take public transport home; on 6 June 2024 the Supreme Federal Tribunal rejected her appeal, leaving refusals lawful under ordinary private-premises rules. In the other direction, Florianópolis has a visible LGBTQ tourism scene with pride events and legal infrastructure accustomed to processing same-sex marriages and marker changes; nationwide legal rights are identical, so visitors see the same federal protections as elsewhere. Caveat: state violence statistics sit atop the country's nationally leading lethality and should be read partly as reporting density rather than as gender-specific exposure.

sources.summary: Encyclopedia overview of LGBT rights in Brazil: the 2011 Supreme Federal Court stable-union ruling; nationwide same-sex marriage via National Council of Justice Resolution 175/2013 (binding on all civil registry offices); the June 2019 Supreme Federal Court decision making homophobia and transphobia punishable under the anti-racism statute (imprisonment 1-5 years plus loss of public office); and gender-marker changes by self-determination.

Outright International country profile (updated 2026): over 3,000 openly LGBTQ candidates ran in the 2024 municipal elections; gender markers changeable by self-determination and trans voters may register with their lived identity; a national intersex human-rights working group installed in December 2023 with recommendations published October 2025; the national LGBTI+ health technical committee reinstated September 2025; a Superior Court of Justice ruling letting nonbinary people amend civil registry; and a proposed National LGBTQIA+ Rights policy running alongside a conservative legislative surge in congress.

LGBTQ+ law-firm guide for expatriates considering relocation to Brazil: legal framework overview — the 2011 stable-union ruling, CNJ Resolution 175/2013, and the 2019 ruling treating homophobia and transphobia as crimes equivalent to racism (1-5 years plus loss of public office), plus property, inheritance and immigration treatment of same-sex spouses; major cities including Florianópolis are broadly welcoming with pride events and established legal infrastructure, smaller towns may show more social friction though legal rights are identical nationwide.

13589884B3780741375954.summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): Antioquia (incl. Medellín and Bello): by a wide margin the country's most lethal department for LGBTIQ people. Regional evidence: 45 of the 270 LGBTIQ+ killings recorded nationally in 2025 occurred here; the director of Caribe Afirmativo presented the department as one of the most dangerous for LGBTIQ+ people in the country; reporting covering part of the year states that more than half of the country's murders of this population took place in the department, three of them in the municipality of Bello. Emblematic case: Sara Millerey González Borja, 32, a trans woman, beaten and thrown into a creek in Bello on 4 April 2025 while onlookers filmed her; she died of her injuries, triggering vigils and a national alert about rising transfeminicides. 1811400B15614733245507.summary: Region research direction: worse than national on public-festival access screening — religion-based identity verification doubles as an outing mechanism for gender-nonconforming visitors. 68945753B55100681051852.name: Seoul
68945753B55100681051852.summary: Region research direction: worse than its reputation — the capital's own council has twice voted to delete anti-discrimination protection, and Pride is contested by the city. (1) 26 April 2024: the Seoul Metropolitan Council passed a bill abolishing the Seoul Student Human Rights Ordinance — 12 years after its promulgation — which had prohibited teachers from discriminating on grounds including gender, sexual orientation and gender identity; the council is controlled by the conservative governing party; abolition triggered protests, the identical bill has now passed a second time and the matter is before the Supreme Court; UN special procedures transmitted a communication on the repeal, with education offices filing observations as enforcing authorities. (2) Pride as contested civic space: the city's mayor uses municipal power against LGBTQ+ gatherings, and the city hosted a mass anti-LGBTQ+ rally claiming 1.1 million participants (organisers, police estimates lower) — described as the largest religious gathering in the country's history. Counterweight: the opposition parliamentary majority announced national student-rights legislation overriding regional offices' decisions, so the repeal is contested and may be undone at national level. Courts from this record's sources: (a) the Seoul Central District Court held that police advice telling a trans person mid-registration-change to "avoid public restrooms for a while" infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won (about $240) of a 3 million won claim, final 2 July 2024, calling comfortable restroom use "a fundamental and universal human right"; a national human rights commission survey (2021, 591 trans respondents) found 41% had used a restroom of a different gender than their identity out of fear of unfair treatment, 39% avoided food and drink to avoid restrooms and 36% went without; a 2021 regional district court awarded 7 million won in damages against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use; (b) a regional court approved gender change for five transgender people without reassignment surgery (8 May 2024), holding that mandatory surgery violates bodily integrity and downgrading prior surgical guidelines to reference status. Model-estimate residual (route 3): largest scene in the country, court protection of the annual queer festival.

Also reports a 2021 NHRCK survey (591 trans respondents: 41% used another-gender restroom out of fear, 39% avoided food/drink, 36% skipped restroom use) and a 2021 Daegu District Court (Pohang branch) ruling awarding 7 million won against a beauty academy that barred a trans student's restroom use.

31927357B30293642818187.name: Quintana Roo
31927357B30293642818187.summary: Quintana Roo: worse than national for what a visitor actually meets — the country's main tourist corridor, with a documented policing problem. The Cancún/Riviera Maya hotel zone is a massive international tourism envelope with a commercially gay-friendly surface, but municipal and state police have been repeatedly documented committing discriminatory acts against LGBT+ people, with multiple recorded assaults during detention concentrated in Tulum and Playa del Carmen; the community describes officers as untrained in human-rights standards. The municipal Directorate for Sexual Diversity recorded three formal discrimination complaints in a single year, including violence against a transgender woman, and two Tourist Police members were fired after their own body cameras showed them running an extortion ring against visitors with portable card terminals. Cancún's immigration detention facility is documented as a place of systematic rights violations with no accountability — relevant to a visitor whose documents are questioned. Countervailing: the state enacted legal gender recognition in 2020 and banned conversion practices in December 2023. Scored relative to the national score (0.55) for Mexico.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch feature (31 March 2025), 'Trans Rights in Mexico: Progress and Challenges'. Country-wide survey of legal gender recognition: 22 of 32 states had legislated an LGR procedure by March 2025, while six states (Aguascalientes, Chiapas, Durango, Querétaro, Tabasco, Tamaulipas) had reformed nothing, leaving trans people's documents permanently mismatched; also documents coercive detention and border scrutiny risks for document-mismatched travellers.

Human Rights Watch report (6 March 2024), 'I Just Want to Contribute to Society: Mexico's Trans People Denied Legal Gender Recognition in Tabasco'. Interviews with trans people in Tabasco about daily discrimination, harassment and differential treatment; highlights the August 2023 killing of Karina Gómez, a trans woman from Villahermosa, found in the Carrizal River with a concrete block tied to her feet; co-authored with a local community centre.

15666254B89722251658211.name: Selangor
15666254B89722251658211.summary: Worse than national despite the most 'progressive-governed' appearance: the wealthiest, most urbanised state wrapping the federal capital is not a safe harbour. In January 2026 the state government declared it 'will not allow LGBT promotion' and called for an investigation into a 'Glamping with Pride' gathering; in December 2025 the state's sultan used Friday sermons across state mosques to warn Muslims against LGBT practices — the monarchy-plus-religious-bureaucracy channel operating statewide. The state's religious department is the agency that pursued a well-known transgender entrepreneur with an arrest warrant and an all-out manhunt over her presentation, mobilising 122 religious affairs officers, which made this state the most visible arena for cross-dressing enforcement nationally. Countervailing: it also has the strongest documented prosecution record for violence against trans people — after a 32-year-old trans woman was beaten to death in Klang in 2018, four suspects were arrested and charged. Scored relative to the national score (0.16) for Malaysia.

1875124B65618634887963.name: Lima
1875124B65618634887963.summary: Worse than national — the top homicide venue in the state's own data, and the site of 2025 killings. The Public Ministry's study of LGTB homicides 2012–2021 identified 84 criminal complaints, 88 victims and 72 identified perpetrators, and found 58% of the deaths occurred in six fiscal districts, led by Lima (12) and La Libertad (10), with Lima Norte among them; Lima Centro also concentrates the highest national frequency of reported crimes overall (10.0%; eleven fiscal districts hold 62%). On 24–28 August 2025 a trans woman reported missing in Independencia (northern Lima) was found dead in her own home four days later; market colleagues and relatives publicly demanded justice. On the law side, congress approved a norm in February 2025 restricting trans people's access to public bathrooms — analysed by a national human-rights institute as 'legalised discrimination' — and a 2024 rights-observatory report counted 54 LGBTI+ murders 2020–2023, with trans women most affected.
